# How Bumpy? (howbumpy.com)

> How Bumpy? is a free, just-for-fun ride comfort meter that runs in the browser. Fix a phone in place on a train, tram, bus, car, plane or boat (in a phone holder or mount, or a seat-back pocket) or clip it to a bike's handlebars, tap Start, and it shows a live comfort gauge; at the end it gives a verdict, a timeline of the ride, the biggest jolts and a seasickness dose. It uses the comfort weightings from ISO 2631-1:1997, but a phone isn't a calibrated instrument and this isn't a certified measurement: it is best for comparing your own rides with the same phone in the same spot. Never use it for safety, health or work-exposure decisions.

How it works: the phone's motion sensor (the browser's devicemotion readings) is resampled onto an even grid, split into up-and-down (along gravity) and horizontal shaking, and weighted in the frequency domain with ISO 2631-1's Wk (vertical) and Wd (horizontal) comfort weightings, k = 1 on every axis. The result is one number in m/s², labelled with the standard's overlapping comfort descriptions (from "Not uncomfortable" under 0.315 m/s² to "Extremely uncomfortable" over 2 m/s²). Moments when the phone is picked up are detected from how fast the gravity direction swings and left out, as are gaps in the readings. The report also gives the roughest 5 seconds, the vibration dose value (which, unlike the main number, changes with which way the phone faces, so compare it only with the phone square to the vehicle and facing the same way) and crest factor, and a motion-sickness dose (Wf weighting). The standard's rough rule for the share of adults that dose would make vomit was worked out for slow up-and-down motion, mostly at sea, so it is shown only when a ride's slow swaying was mostly up and down, after 20 minutes or more of usable readings, rounded and never above "more than 30%", and never for cars, buses or bikes.

Output: a shareable 1080×1080 image card (which carries the "just for fun, not certified" line), a CSV of the resampled signals for a fresh ride, and a list of saved rides (up to 60) sortable smoothest or roughest first. A simulated sample tram ride shows the report on devices without a motion sensor.

Privacy: everything is computed on the phone. Nothing is uploaded, no location is used, there are no cookies or analytics; saved rides stay in the browser's local storage. It is an installable PWA and works offline once opened.

Technical: static files only (index.html, style.css, app.js, comfort.js for the maths, ride-worker.js to work out a finished ride off the page's main thread, sw.js), MIT-licensed, no build step, no backend.
